steps.say: Two very different tumours are grouped under this name, divided by age. Children grow a cystic chalky mass driven by one gene, while adults grow a solid mass driven by another. Knowing which type it is changes the whole treatment, because the adult type can melt with targeted pills.
steps.tx: The childhood form, **adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma** (chalky cystic tumour), grows as calcified suprasellar lumps filled with machine-oil fluid, switched on by **CTNNB1** (beta-catenin gene) mutations. The adult papillary form instead carries **BRAF V600E** (targetable kinase mutation), so age plus genetics splits one name into two diseases with different treatments.

steps.say: A child who stops growing, starts missing the sides of vision and carries chalk on the scan has this tumour until proven otherwise. The combination of short stature, half-gone visual fields and a calcified cyst above the pituitary is almost diagnostic. Pituitary adenomas and simple cysts look different.
steps.tx: A calcified suprasellar cyst plus **bitemporal hemianopia** (both outer visual fields lost) and **growth failure** (stopped height gain) in a child is craniopharyngioma until proven otherwise. **Suprasellar calcification** (chalk above the pituitary) separates it from pituitary adenoma and **Rathke cyst** (benign pouch remnant), which lack chunky calcium with stunted growth.

vis.caption: Sagittal sellar anatomy: pituitary adenoma shown; craniopharyngioma sits above with calcified cyst. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The tragedy of this tumour is not the lump but what surrounds it. The hunger centre, the water-balance centre and the hormone master switch are all packed within millimetres. Modern surgeons therefore leave the stuck rim behind and finish with radiation rather than injure the hypothalamus chasing total removal.
steps.tx: **Hypothalamic obesity** (uncontrollable weight gain), **diabetes insipidus** (water-loss disorder) and panhypopituitarism dominate morbidity, so modern strategy favours safe **subtotal resection** (planned partial removal) with radiotherapy over hypothalamus-injuring gross total removal. Protecting the hypothalamus matters more than clearing every cell, since hypothalamic injury is often permanent and difficult to treat.

steps.say: Adults with the papillary type have a remarkable option their childhood counterparts lack. Two pills that block the mutated pathway can shrink the tumour before any knife is used. Surgeons then remove a smaller, softer remnant with far less risk.
steps.tx: Papillary **BRAF-mutant** (kinase-mutated) tumours respond to **dabrafenib** (BRAF blocker) plus **trametinib** (MEK blocker), allowing **neoadjuvant** (pre-surgery shrinkage) treatment before conservative surgery in selected adults. Targeted shrinkage converts a formidable skull-base operation into a safer limited resection with the mutation doing the heavy work.

steps.say: The cyst often refills after surgery, especially in children where repeat operations are costly. A small reservoir left under the scalp lets doctors draw off fluid and inject medicine directly into the cyst. This buys years of control while the child grows.
steps.tx: Cystic recurrences are managed through an **Ommaya reservoir** (scalp fluid port) with intracavitary **interferon alpha** (cyst-wall drug), deferring reoperation and radiotherapy in the growing child. Draining and dosing the **cystic recurrence** (refilled tumour cyst) through the port controls pressure without reopening the skull each time.

steps.say: When radiation is needed in a child, the beam type matters enormously for the developing brain. Proton beams stop at the target instead of passing through, sparing memory, hearing and hormones beyond. Photon beams are scattered further and are linked with more late damage.
steps.tx: **Proton therapy** (stopping-beam radiation) is preferred for residual disease in children to spare **cognition** (learning ability), hearing and the **hypothalamic axis** (hormone control pathway) compared with photon therapy. **Cognition sparing** (protecting learning) plus preserved hormones and hearing make protons worth the travel, since a cured child lives decades with the beam's after-effects.

steps.say: Not every lump above the pituitary is this tumour. A smooth bony-base growth with an enhancing tail and no chalky cyst points to a meningioma instead. That changes the operation completely, because surgeons remove the tumour with its dural attachment and any involved bone where safe.
steps.tx: **Tuberculum sellae** (bony ridge) and planum **meningiomas** (dural tumours) mimic craniopharyngioma but show a **dural tail** (enhancing dural flare) and homogeneous enhancement without calcified cysts. Recognition changes the operation to **Simpson resection** (tumour plus dural origin removal), since leaving the dural attachment raises recurrence risk.

steps.say: Cure of the lump is only the start of lifelong care. Hormones, vision, sleep, weight, school performance and blood vessels all need watching forever. Late strokes and second tumours from old radiation can appear decades later, so these patients are never discharged.
steps.tx: Lifelong endocrine, visual, sleep and **neurocognitive surveillance** (thinking-skill checks) follows every craniopharyngioma survivor, because **late effects** (delayed harms) are common. Hypothalamic weight gain, vascular events and **second tumour** (radiation-induced new cancer) risks persist for decades, so follow-up is shared between endocrinology, eyes, sleep and school support.
